source.title: When Structured Sparse Autoencoders Learn Consistent Concepts Across Modalities
source.authors: Wei-Duo Liao; Yunqiao Yang; Ying Wei

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures whether an SAE can recover semantically interpretable sparse features in a vision-language model, using feature-alignment and monosemanticity measures rather than the toy-network geometry studied in the original work.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on SAE feature alignment, monosemanticity, and cross-modal consistency. Results cited from prior work are not recorded. Hyperparameter-selection and clustering comparisons are not included unless they report a feature-related outcome.
record.test_reason: The paper uses SAEs as an interpretability tool on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and proposes a structured-sparsity variant (S²AE). Its results compare its own method with a vanilla TopK SAE on alignment, sparsity and monosemanticity. It does not test whether the VLM's representations are superposed, whether SAE-recoverable sparse features exist as a property of the model, or any toy-model, capacity, canonicity or dimensionality claim. Residual polysemanticity in SAE features is taken as given and treated as something to fix.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that S²AE's structured sparsity regularizers (exclusive + group sparsity over attention/spatial patch clusters) improve SAE visual concept alignment (mIoU^c) and sparsity in Qwen2.5-VL-7B while keeping EV >0.99. They also argue that the benefit propagates to language-side monosemanticity and cross-modal consistency through the shared dictionary. In addition, they claim their hierarchical VLM→LLM interpretation pipeline is more reliable than direct VLM summarization.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains structured sparse autoencoders with visual-region grouping, exclusive sparsity, and group sparsity; it does not reproduce the original toy-network setup or its geometric measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary by layer and by regularizer combination. Exclusive sparsity alone increases cluster-level alignment but reduces within-group consistency; adding group sparsity partly restores that consistency. The paper also reports that clustering choices and α affect cluster quality.

fits_no_version.finding: Vanilla TopK SAE features on Qwen2.5-VL-7B are mostly summarizable by an LLM pipeline (identification rate about 0.97–0.99). However, multimodal features have low vision monosemanticity (about 0.49–0.51) and low cross-modal consistency (about 0.29–0.33) (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features in VLM residual streams are largely nameable but often visually polysemantic and cross-modally inconsistent.

record.problems: Evidence is from one VLM. Feature interpretation and consistency use automated Qwen models, and visual clusters are derived from the model's attention and spatial structure rather than independent ground-truth labels. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the listed comparisons.

untested.parts: No toy models, geometry or sparsity transition.
No test of capacity as the cause of polysemanticity.
No analysis of the causes of native-neuron polysemanticity.
Does not test whether Qwen2.5-VL spreads features across neurons or whether sparse features exist. SAEs are used as a tool, and only method-vs-method comparisons are reported.
No completeness, stability across seeds, or canonicity tests.

record.verdict_notes: This is a methods paper on SAE variants. Every recorded row compares the authors' S²AE with a vanilla SAE or ablates its regularizers, so none bear on a superposition version. Further problems: the 'ground-truth' clusters come from the model's own attention, monosemanticity is judged with automated Qwen/SigLip pipelines, and no uncertainty is reported. The original paper is cited only in the related-work and introduction sections.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network test of overlapping directions, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
Does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by limited network capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not investigate causes of polysemanticity in the model's native neurons independent of capacity pressure.
Tests SAE-recovered features in one vision-language model; does not establish how features are distributed across native neurons in other LLMs.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable across runs, or canonical units of representation.
Does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.

relation.reason: Sparse feature decomposition supplies the interpretability framework; the reported comparisons measure alignment, monosemanticity, consistency, reconstruction and sparsity improvements of the proposed method.

tranche.reason: The study uses SAE decomposition and evaluates its proposed regularizers and interpretation pipeline against vanilla SAEs. Its results concern its own method's performance, without independently testing a listed claim version.

source_check.notes: All sampled values and conditions match the text. These are method-performance rows, not claim-test evidence; alignment targets use attention/spatial clusters, Table 2 leaves layer unspecified, and the vanilla L0 baseline is fixed by K=256.

reader_labels.reason: SAE features show measurable alignment with visual clusters and improved monosemanticity or cross-modal consistency under structured training; see r1-r13 and r16-r22.
